title: Quantum Computing, Simply

endcard.line: Pictures: National Institute of Standards and Technology (public domain)

segments.say: This lab hardware holds single charged atoms in place, and each atom can act as a quantum bit. Here is why that matters.
An ordinary bit is like a switch: zero or one. A qubit can be in a blend of both at once. Physicists call this superposition.
Qubits can also be entangled, linked so that measuring one tells you about the other. Together, these let some problems be solved in new ways.
But qubits are fragile. Heat and noise knock them out of their state, so today's machines make many errors, and many must be kept extremely cold.
They are expected to work alongside ordinary computers, not replace them, on problems like new materials, medicines and security. They could also break some of today's encryption.

segments.say: India approved its National Quantum Mission in twenty twenty-three, at about six thousand crore rupees, aiming for computers of fifty to a thousand qubits within eight years.
For GS Three, know superposition, entanglement, and why the world is now building post-quantum cryptography.
